a: the Righteous One
p: The printed Ethiopic texts speak of a person, "the Righteous One"; some manuscripts, as Charles and Knibb report, have "righteousness."

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
Some Ethiopic manuscripts, as reported in the editions of Charles and Knibb (their apparatus was not rechecked here)

why: The two words differ by one vowel in Ge'ez. "The Righteous One" fits the parallel "the Righteous and Chosen One" in 53:6 and is read by most editors; "righteousness" may be a scribe's slip, or an easier reading.

a: the place of the chosen ones of righteousness and faith
t: The chosen ones, or the Chosen One?
p: Dillmann's text and the EOTC Bible have the plural. Charles and many modern versions read "the Chosen One." Goes with the entries on "their days" (39:6) and "their homes" (39:7).

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
readings.orig: መካነ ፡ ኅሩያን ፡ ዘጽድቅ ፡ ወዘሃይማኖት (mäkanä ḫəruyan zäṣədq wäzähaymanot)
readings.en: the place of the chosen ones of righteousness and faith
readings.plain: the place of the chosen ones of righteousness and faith

readings.w: Other Ethiopic manuscripts, as reported by Charles (1906, 1912) and followed by most modern translations; which manuscript family reads it was not checked here
readings.orig: (the singular, ḫəruy; exact wording not checked)
readings.en: the Chosen One of righteousness and faith
readings.plain: the Chosen One of righteousness and faith

why: The Plain follows the printed Ethiopic texts. Whether the older Ethiopic I manuscripts (such as EMML 2080 and Tana 9) have the singular would decide the question, and that has not been checked here; if they do, the singular should be preferred. If the singular is right, this is the first appearance of the Chosen One in the book, and 39:6–7 would speak of "his days" and "his dwelling." Many scholars prefer the singular because the next chapters build on it; the plural fits the context of the homes of the righteous in 39:4–5.

a: Righteousness will fill their days
p: Goes with the 39:6 entry on "the chosen ones": if the Chosen One is meant, this line speaks of "his days."

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
readings.en: and righteousness will be in their days

readings.w: Charles (1912), with the singular "Chosen One"; not rechecked here
readings.en: righteousness will prevail in his days

why: This stands or falls with the reading "the chosen ones" earlier in the verse. Both printed Ethiopic texts are plural throughout.

a: I saw their homes
p: Goes with the two entries at 39:6.

readings.w: Charles (1912), with the singular "Chosen One"; not rechecked here

why: Both Ethiopic texts are plural ("their"); they differ only in the form of the noun. The singular belongs with Charles's reading "the Chosen One" at 39:6.

a: repentance and hope
t: Repentance and hope, or repentance leading to hope?
p: A small difference: Dillmann joins the two with "and."
why: Both make Phanuel the angel who leads people to repent; the EOTC wording makes hope the result of repentance. The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: before the world was created, and forever
p: Dillmann's text adds "and forever in his presence"; the EOTC Bible lacks it.

readings.plain: before the world was created, and forever

why: The longer text says the Son of Man stays hidden with God for ever, not only before creation. The Plain follows Dillmann, who is supported by Charles.

a: there will be rest on the earth
p: Dillmann's text has "rest"; the EOTC Bible has "fear."

readings.plain: there will be rest on the earth
there will be fear on the earth

why: Both make sense. "Rest" means that when the oppressors fall the earth is at peace, as in Isaiah 14:7 after the tyrant's fall. "Fear" means the day is terrible for them. The Plain follows Dillmann; Charles also reads "rest."

a: They will have no honor
p: The EOTC Bible drops the "not": the others "will have honor."

readings.en: and they will have no honor

why: The difference is one letter, but it changes the status of "the others": in Dillmann's text they are saved without honor, by mercy alone; in the EOTC text they are honored too. Dillmann's reading fits the contrast with the righteous in 50:1–2 and is followed by Charles. The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: on his throne
p: The Ethiopic texts say "his throne." Charles reads "my throne" (God's).

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
Charles's edition (1912), reading God as the speaker; whether he followed a manuscript or a conjecture was not checked here

why: The Plain follows the Ethiopic. Elsewhere the Chosen One sits on God's throne (61:8; 62:2 as Charles reads it), so Charles thought God must be speaking here. But the passage is not in God's voice, and "his throne" makes sense.

a: the throne of my glory
p: Dillmann has God call it "my" throne; the EOTC Bible has "his."
why: God is speaking (55:3), so "my glory" makes the Chosen One sit on God's own throne, a bold claim found also in 61:8. "His glory" is the more usual phrase of the Parables (62:5; 69:29) and may be a scribe smoothing the text. The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: for those who bow to the righteous judgment
p: Charles added "not." Dillmann's text and the EOTC Bible do not have it.

readings.w: Dillmann's text (the EOTC Bible agrees, spelling the word ለኵነኔ)
readings.orig: ለእለ ፡ ይሰግዱ ፡ ለኲነኔ ፡ ጽድቅ (läʾəlla yəsägədu läkʷənnane ṣədq)
readings.en: for those who bow to the righteous judgment
readings.plain: for those who bow to the righteous judgment

readings.orig: for those who do not bow to the righteous law
readings.en: for those who do not bow to the righteous judgment
readings.plain: for those who do not bow to the righteous judgment

why: Without "not" the verse is awkward, since punishment seems to be prepared for the faithful, and most translators supply it. It can be read only if the end of the verse applies to each group in turn: a covenant for those who honor God's judgment and an inquiry for those who deny it. The Plain keeps the Ethiopic texts and notes the difficulty.

a: All his holy ones in heaven will bless him, and
t: A line missing in the EOTC text
p: Dillmann's text has a line that the EOTC Bible lacks.

readings.orig: ይባርክዎ ፡ ኲሎሙ ፡ ቅዱሳኑ ፡ እለ ፡ ውስተ ፡ ሰማይ (yəbarkəwo kʷəllomu qədusanu ʾəlla wəstä sämay)
readings.en: all his holy ones who are in heaven will bless him
readings.plain: All his holy ones in heaven will bless him, and

why: The two lines begin the same way ("will bless him... in heaven"), so a copyist's eye could easily skip from one to the other. That explains the shorter text better than an addition would. The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: The Lord of Spirits sat on the throne of his glory
p: Dillmann's text and the EOTC Bible say the Lord of Spirits sat. Many editors read "seated him" (the Chosen One).

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
readings.plain: The Lord of Spirits sat on the throne of his glory

readings.w: Charles (1912) and many modern translations, by a small change (ʾanbäro, "seated him")
readings.en: The Lord of Spirits seated him
readings.plain: The Lord of Spirits seated him on the throne of his glory

why: The Plain follows the manuscripts. The emendation is attractive because the rest of the verse (the spirit poured on him, the word of his mouth) describes the Chosen One, as in 61:8, where the Ge'ez does say "seated." But both printed Ethiopic texts read "sat." Read strictly, the rest of the verse then speaks of God (see the note on "on him").

a: that Son of a Woman
t: Son of a Woman, or Son of Man?
p: Dillmann's text and the EOTC Bible read "son of a woman" here.

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
Some manuscripts, as reported in Charles's edition (not rechecked here), and most translations

why: The two words differ by one letter. "Son of a Woman" is the harder reading and is what both printed Ethiopic texts have, so the Plain keeps it. Christian copyists may have liked it as a hint of the virgin birth; others think it was a slip for "son of a man." Either way, it is the same figure as "that Son of Man" elsewhere.

a: the sword of the Lord of Spirits
p: Dillmann has "sword"; the EOTC Bible has "punishment."

readings.plain: the sword of the Lord of Spirits
the punishment of the Lord of Spirits

why: "His sword is drunk" is a known prophetic image (Isaiah 34:5; Deuteronomy 32:42); "punishment" is the commoner word in the Parables and may have replaced the bolder image. The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: and eat
p: The EOTC Bible adds "and drink."
why: "Eat and drink" is the natural pair and may be a scribe completing it. The meaning is the same.

a: Because of the months they searched out and learned
p: The Ethiopic says "months." Charles read "sorceries."

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
readings.plain: Because of the months they searched out and learned
Because of the sorceries they searched out and learned

why: Neither Dillmann's text nor the EOTC Bible has "sorceries"; Charles's reading is a conjecture. The Plain keeps "months," which fits the Enochic concern with the moon and the calendar (8:3; 80:2–8).

a: for the healing of the angels and for the death of their bodies
t: Healing for the angels, or for the kings?
p: Neither Ethiopic text has "kings" or "lust"; those words come from Charles's emendation.

readings.orig: ለፈውሰ ፡ ዚአሆሙ ፡ ለመላእክት ፡ ወለሞተ ፡ ሥጋሆሙ (läfäwsä ziʾähomu lämälaʾəkt wälämotä śəgahomu)
readings.en: for their healing, of the angels, and for the death of their body
readings.plain: for the healing of the angels and for the death of their bodies

readings.orig: ለፈውሰ፡ ሥጋሆሙ፡ (läfäwsä śəgahomu lämälaʾəkt wälämotä śəgahomu)
readings.en: for the healing of their body, of the angels, and for the death of their body
readings.plain: for the healing of the angels' bodies and for the death of their bodies

readings.en: for the healing of the body of the kings and the lust of their body
readings.plain: for the healing of the bodies of the kings and for the lust of their bodies

why: Charles found healing for the angels out of place in a passage about the kings and their baths (67:8–12) and rewrote the line. No witness known to us reads "kings." The Plain keeps the Ethiopic and explains the crux in the note.

a: Izezeel
p: The twenty-first name differs: Dillmann has Izezeel; the EOTC Bible repeats Azazel.
why: Azazel is already tenth on the list, so naming him again as twenty-first is unlikely to be original. "Izezeel" is probably a garbled name; the Aramaic list in 6:7 has twenty names, so the twenty-first may have come in by a copying error.

a: the word of that Son of Man will be strong
p: The EOTC Bible reads "they will tell that Son of Man."

readings.w: Dillmann's text (wänägäfu, an unclear word that Charles and others read as nägäru, "his word")
readings.orig: ወነገፉ ፡ ለውእቱ ፡ ወልደ ፡ ብእሲ ፡ ይጸንዕ (wänägäfu läwəʾətu wäldä bəʾəsi yəṣänəʿ)
readings.en: and the word of that son of man will be strong
readings.plain: the word of that Son of Man will be strong

readings.orig: ወይነግሩ ፡ ለውእቱ ፡ ወልደ ፡ ብእሲ ፡ ወይጸንዕ (wäyənägəru läwəʾətu wäldä bəʾəsi wäyəṣänəʿ)
readings.en: and they will speak to that son of man, and he will be strong
readings.plain: they will speak to that Son of Man, and he will be strong

why: Dillmann's word is unclear, and the EOTC reading may be a scribe's attempt to make sense of it. The Plain follows the common reading "his word" (compare 62:2), with Charles.

a: his name was lifted up into the presence of that Son of Man and into the presence of the Lord of Spirits
t: Raised to the Son of Man, or raised as the Son of Man?
p: One early manuscript lacks "into the presence of" and so makes Enoch's name "that Son of Man."

readings.w: Dillmann's text (the EOTC Bible has the same words, but joins the last phrase with "and")
readings.orig: ተለዐለ ፡ ስሙ ፡ ሕያው ፡ በኀቤሁ ፡ ለውእቱ ፡ ወልደ ፡ እጓለ ፡ እመሕያው ፡ በኀበ ፡ እግዚአ ፡ መናፍስት (täläʿälä səmu ḥəyaw bäḫabehu läwəʾətu wäldä ʾəgʷalä ʾəmmäḥəyaw bäḫäbä ʾƎgziʾa Mänafəst)
readings.en: his name was lifted up alive to the presence of that Son of Man, to the presence of the Lord of Spirits
readings.plain: his name was lifted up into the presence of that Son of Man and into the presence of the Lord of Spirits

readings.w: EMML 2080 (15th century, Ethiopic I), as reported in Knibb's apparatus (1978) and argued by Olson (1998; 2009)
readings.en: the name of that Son of Man was lifted up alive to the Lord of Spirits
readings.plain: the name of that Son of Man was lifted up into the presence of the Lord of Spirits

why: The longer text has Enoch taken up to the Son of Man, a separate figure, and then in 71:14 told that he is the Son of Man, which is hard to fit together. The shorter text, from a manuscript of the older "Ethiopic I" family, says that the name of the Son of Man, meaning Enoch, was lifted up, which agrees with 71:14. Olson argues for it; Nickelsburg and VanderKam keep the longer text, and Olson himself grants that manuscripts alone cannot settle it. The Plain keeps the reading of Dillmann and the EOTC Bible.
b: The variant matters for the debate over 71:14 (see the note there). If the shorter reading is original, the whole ending of the Parables identifies Enoch with the Son of Man; if the longer reading is original, 70:1 keeps them apart and 71:14 stands alone. A smaller difference: Dillmann has bäḫäbä, "to," before "the Lord of Spirits"; the EOTC Bible has wäḫäbä, "and to."

a: seraphim, cherubim and ophanim
t: The order of the angel ranks
p: The EOTC Bible puts the cherubim first.

readings.orig: ወዐውዱ ፡ ሱራፌል ፡ ወኪሩቤል ፡ ወኦፍኒን (wäʿäwdu surafel wäkirubel wäʾofnin)
readings.en: and around it, seraphim and cherubim and ophanim

readings.orig: በዐውዱ፡ ኪሩቤል፡ ወሱራፌል፡ ወአፍኒን፡ (bäʿäwdu kirubel wäsurafel wäʾäfnin)
readings.en: around it, cherubim and seraphim and ophanim

why: The meaning is the same. The EOTC order matches 61:10 (cherubim, seraphim, ophanim). The Plain follows Dillmann.

a: You are the Son of Man
t: "You are the Son of Man": the manuscripts and Charles's change
p: The Ethiopic texts have the angel say to Enoch, "You are the Son of Man."

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
readings.orig: አንተ ፡ ውእቱ ፡ ወልደ ፡ ብእሲ (ʾantä wəʾətu wäldä bəʾəsi)
readings.en: You are the son of man
readings.plain: You are the Son of Man

readings.w: Charles (1912), a conjecture that changes the person in 71:14–17
readings.orig: This is the Son of Man
readings.en: This is the Son of Man
readings.plain: This is the Son of Man

why: No witness known to us supports Charles's change. He made it because he could not believe the book would call Enoch the Son of Man after describing the Son of Man as someone Enoch saw beside God (46:1). Almost all scholars since Knibb (1978) translate the text as it stands and argue about what it means, not about what it says. No Aramaic or Greek survives to check the Ethiopic.
b: Charles also changed "you" to "him" in 71:15–16 to match. The Plain keeps the second person there as well. The views on what the verse means are in the note on 71:14.

a: walk on your path
p: The Ethiopic speaks to Enoch ("your path"). Charles changed it to "his ways."

readings.w: Dillmann's text and the EOTC printed Bible
Charles (1912), a conjecture to match his change in 71:14

why: This goes with the variant at 71:14. The Plain keeps the manuscripts.
